questions.question: Why is every Jordan block upper triangular?
options: Its only nonzero entries lie on the main diagonal.
All entries below the main diagonal are zero.
It is symmetric, so both triangles match.
All entries above the diagonal are zero.

questions.question: Which matrix is a $2\times2$ Jordan block with eigenvalue 4?
How is a $1\times1$ Jordan block different from a larger block?
options: It is $(1)$ for every eigenvalue, like an identity block.
It cannot appear in a Jordan normal form.
It is just $(λ)$ and has no superdiagonal 1s.
It is $(\lambda)$ with a single superdiagonal $1$.

questions.question: Why can the eigenvalues of a Jordan block be read from its diagonal?
options: It is symmetric, and symmetric matrices have diagonal eigenvalues.
It is upper triangular, so the diagonal holds its eigenvalues.
Its trace equals the eigenvalue sum, so each diagonal entry is an eigenvalue.
Its $1$s above the diagonal are eigenvalues as well, next to $\lambda$.

questions.question: What is the characteristic polynomial of $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$?
A Jordan normal form may contain several Jordan blocks for the same eigenvalue $\lambda$. Which quantity always equals the size of one particular block for $\lambda$?
options: The length of the Jordan chain that block comes from
The algebraic multiplicity of $\lambda$ for the whole matrix
The number of independent eigenvectors for $\lambda$ in the whole matrix
The number of distinct eigenvalues of the whole matrix

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{J}=\boldsymbol{J}(\lambda)$ be a $3\times3$ Jordan block. What are the algebraic and geometric multiplicities of $\lambda$, and is $\boldsymbol{J}$ diagonalizable?

A Jordan chain $(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\boldsymbol{v}_3)$ of $\boldsymbol{A}$ for $\lambda$ satisfies $(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}_3=\boldsymbol{v}_2$, $(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{v}_1$, $(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}_1=\boldsymbol{0}$. In the basis $(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\boldsymbol{v}_3)$, what is the second column of the matrix of $\boldsymbol{A}$?

A $3\times3$ matrix $\boldsymbol{A}$ has a Jordan chain $(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\boldsymbol{v}_3)$ for $\lambda$: $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}_1=\lambda\boldsymbol{v}_1$, $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}_2=\lambda\boldsymbol{v}_2+\boldsymbol{v}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}_3=\lambda\boldsymbol{v}_3+\boldsymbol{v}_2$. What is the matrix of $\boldsymbol{A}$ in the reversed basis $(\boldsymbol{v}_3,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\boldsymbol{v}_1)$?

Let $\boldsymbol{A}$ be a square matrix with eigenvalue $\lambda$, and let $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2$ be vectors with $(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{v}_1$ and $(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}_1=\boldsymbol{0}$. When is $(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2)$ a Jordan chain of length $2$?
options: Always, since both chain relations already hold
Exactly when $\boldsymbol{v}_2$ is an eigenvector for $\lambda$ as well
Exactly when the vector $\boldsymbol{v}_2$ is nonzero
Exactly when the vector $\boldsymbol{v}_1$ is nonzero
